column2: feeling your face go hot and your fists clench after a brother takes your things
column3: stop, take a few slow deep breaths and count to ten before you say or do anything
column4: anger makes the body ready to fight and the thinking part of the brain catches up only after a few seconds

column2: wanting to hit someone who made you furious
column3: never hit; walk away, squeeze a pillow, stamp your feet outside or tell an adult instead
column4: hitting hurts people and gets you into trouble, and the anger still needs to go somewhere safe

column2: shouting a mean word at your mum when she says no to a screen
column3: go somewhere quiet to calm down, then come back and say sorry for the word
column4: angry words can hurt for a long time, and saying sorry repairs the trust

column2: slamming your bedroom door in a rage
column3: close the door gently and use your words once you are calm
column4: slamming can trap fingers, break things and frighten others in the house

column2: being angry at a game that keeps beating you
column3: take a break, get a drink of water and come back later
column4: a tired, angry brain plays worse, and a pause lets you think of a new way

column2: feeling angry because something is truly unfair
column3: say calmly what is unfair and what you would like to happen instead
column4: people listen to a calm, clear reason much more than to a shout

column2: a friend says you always get angry too fast
column3: notice your early warning signs (tight chest, hot face) and use them as a signal to pause
column4: the earlier you catch anger, the easier it is to calm down

column2: breaking a toy on purpose because you were furious
column3: tell an adult what happened and think about how to make it right
column4: owning up teaches you to control anger next time and keeps people's trust

column2: wanting to get revenge on a classmate who tripped you
column3: tell a teacher instead of planning payback
column4: revenge usually makes the fight bigger and gets both of you into trouble

column2: staying angry at someone for days
column3: talk it through with them or a trusted adult and try to forgive
column4: holding on to anger keeps you unhappy long after the problem is over

column2: being scared of a big dog barking behind a fence
column3: stay calm, walk past slowly without staring or running
column4: running can make a dog chase you, and the fence is there to keep it in

column2: being afraid to go on stage for the school play
column3: practise a lot, breathe slowly before you go on and remember the audience wants you to do well
column4: almost everyone feels stage fright, and it often fades once you start

column2: feeling scared after watching a frightening film
column3: talk about it with a parent and do something calm and cheerful before bed
column4: talking makes the fear smaller, and films are made up with special effects

column2: being frightened of the doctor's needle for a vaccination
column3: tell the nurse you are scared, look away, breathe out slowly and hold a hand
column4: the sting lasts a second and the vaccine protects you from serious illnesses

column2: being afraid of the dentist
column3: ask the dentist to explain what they will do and agree a hand signal to pause
column4: knowing what comes next and having some control makes it much less scary

column2: being scared of thunder and lightning
column3: stay indoors away from windows, count between flash and bang, and keep busy with something cosy
column4: inside a house you are safe, and counting shows the storm moving away

column2: being afraid of spiders or insects
column3: keep your distance, ask an adult to move it outside and learn which local ones are harmless
column4: most are harmless, and knowing the facts shrinks the fear (in Australia some spiders do need an adult)

column2: feeling scared to try swimming in the deep end
column3: learn with a teacher step by step and only swim where an adult is watching
column4: courage grows by small steps, and supervision keeps you safe

column2: being afraid that something bad will happen to your parents
column3: tell them about the worry; they can tell you how they stay safe
column4: worries kept inside grow, and grown-ups can give you real facts

column2: being scared of the news about wars, fires or disasters
column3: ask an adult to explain, and limit how much news you watch
column4: news shows the worst things, and the helpers working on them are often not shown

column2: feeling your heart race and your tummy hurt from fear
column3: breathe in slowly for four, hold for four, out for four
column4: slow breathing tells your body the danger is over

column2: being afraid of being lost in a crowd
column3: agree a meeting place with your family and know to ask a staff member or a parent with children for help
column4: a plan in advance means you know exactly what to do if it happens

column2: lying in bed worrying about a test tomorrow
column3: write the worry down or tell a parent, then remind yourself you have prepared
column4: putting worries on paper or into words helps the brain let them go and sleep

column2: worrying about things that might happen but probably will not
column3: ask yourself how likely it really is and what you could do if it did
column4: worry often makes rare things feel certain

column2: having a worry that will not go away for weeks
column3: tell a parent, teacher or school counsellor
column4: long worries are a real problem that grown-ups can help with, and you do not have to carry them alone

column2: worrying that you did something wrong but not being sure
column3: ask the person or an adult instead of guessing
column4: often the worry is much bigger than what really happened

column2: worrying about grown-up problems like money at home
column3: ask your parents gently; it is their job to sort it out, not yours
column4: children can help a little, but grown-up problems are for grown-ups

column2: using a worry box or worry time
column3: save worries for ten minutes at a set time each day and talk them through
column4: it stops worries from taking over the whole day

column2: feeling sick every morning before school
column3: tell your parents and teacher so they can find out why
column4: tummy aches can be the body's way of showing worry about something at school

column2: feeling sad and not knowing why
column3: let yourself feel it, rest, do something gentle you like and tell someone
column4: everyone feels sad sometimes, and sadness usually passes

column2: wanting to cry at school
column3: it is fine to cry; ask to go somewhere quiet or to a teacher you trust
column4: crying is a normal way the body lets out big feelings, for boys and girls alike

column2: someone says big boys don't cry
column3: know that crying is healthy for everyone
column4: holding feelings in does not make them go away

column2: a friend looks sad and alone at break
column3: go and ask if they are okay and invite them to join you
column4: a small kind act can change someone's whole day

column2: feeling sad for many days and losing interest in things you used to love
column3: tell a parent, teacher or doctor
column4: long sadness can be an illness called depression and it can be helped

column2: feeling so bad that you think about hurting yourself
column3: tell a trusted adult straight away or call a children's helpline
column4: you deserve help, and these feelings can get better with support

column2: cheering yourself up when you feel low
column3: go outside, move your body, hug a pet, listen to music or talk to a friend
column4: exercise, daylight and people lift the mood

column2: the birthday party is cancelled because of rain
column3: say you are disappointed, then help plan another day
column4: naming the feeling helps, and looking forward helps more

column2: not getting picked for the school team
column3: feel the disappointment, ask the coach what to practise and keep trying
column4: many great players were not picked at first

column2: getting a present you did not want
column3: say thank you warmly anyway
column4: the giver thought of you and spent time or money on you

column2: a friend cannot come to your sleepover
column3: tell them it is okay and suggest another date
column4: friends cannot always come, and being understanding keeps the friendship

column2: feeling jealous when your friend plays with someone else
column3: remember friends can have more than one friend and join in or play with others too
column4: friendship is not a prize only one person can own

column2: being jealous of a sibling's new bike
column3: tell a parent how you feel instead of being mean to your sibling
column4: feelings are okay, but taking them out on others is not fair

column2: wishing you had what a classmate has
column3: think about the good things you already have
column4: comparing yourself with others makes you unhappy, gratitude makes you happier

column2: a classmate gets a better mark than you
column3: congratulate them and ask how they studied
column4: being happy for others makes you a good friend and you can learn from them

column2: feeling jealous of a new baby getting all the attention
column3: ask a parent for special time with just you
column4: parents still love you just as much; babies simply need a lot of care

column2: tripping over in front of the whole class
column3: laugh it off, get up and carry on
column4: everyone trips sometimes, and people forget quickly

column2: giving a wrong answer out loud in class
column3: remember that mistakes are how everyone learns
column4: teachers want you to try, and others probably had the same question

column2: calling the teacher Mum by mistake
column3: laugh along; it happens to almost everyone
column4: it is one of the most common slips, and teachers are used to it

column2: having an accident like wetting yourself or being sick at school
column3: tell a teacher quietly; they will help you clean up and get changed
column4: bodies sometimes have accidents, and adults know how to help discreetly

column2: someone laughs when you are embarrassed
column3: walk away and talk to a friend or adult
column4: laughing at someone's embarrassment is unkind, and it is not your fault

column2: seeing a classmate embarrassed
column3: do not laugh or point; say something kind or change the subject
column4: you would want the same kindness

column2: being bored on a rainy day with no screen
column3: build a den, read, draw, write a story, do a puzzle or help cook
column4: boredom is the start of creativity

column2: being bored on a long car journey
column3: play I spy, count number plates, listen to audiobooks or look out of the window
column4: games and stories make the time pass faster

column2: saying I'm bored over and over to a parent
column3: make a list of things you like doing and choose from it
column4: parents are not entertainers, and learning to fill your own time is a skill

column2: being bored in a lesson you find easy
column3: ask the teacher for a harder challenge politely
column4: teachers often have extension work for students who finish early

column2: being too excited to sleep before a birthday or holiday
column3: do something calm like reading and breathe slowly
column4: the day will come quicker if you sleep

column2: getting so excited you run around shouting indoors
column3: go outside to let the energy out or take some deep breaths
column4: indoors other people may be resting, and running inside can cause accidents

column2: being excited and interrupting everyone
column3: wait for a pause in the talk before you speak
column4: people feel respected when they are allowed to finish

column2: feeling proud of a drawing you worked hard on
column3: enjoy the feeling and show it to someone
column4: being proud of effort encourages you to keep improving

column2: winning a race at sports day
column3: smile, thank others and shake hands with the losers
column4: good winners do not boast, and others will be happy for you

column2: losing a match
column3: shake hands, say well played and think about what to practise
column4: good losers are respected, and losing teaches more than winning

column2: showing off about having more toys than others
column3: share the fun instead of boasting
column4: boasting makes others feel small and pushes friends away

column2: being too proud to say sorry
column3: say sorry anyway
column4: saying sorry is brave and makes friendships stronger

column2: not knowing what you are feeling
column3: try to name it: angry, sad, scared, worried, happy, or a mix
column4: naming a feeling makes it easier to manage

column2: having two feelings at once, like excited and nervous
column3: know that mixed feelings are normal
column4: big moments often bring more than one feeling

column2: someone asks how you are and you say fine but you are not
column3: tell a trusted adult how you really feel
column4: people can only help if they know

column2: keeping a feelings diary
column3: write or draw how you felt each day
column4: it helps you spot what makes you happy or upset

column2: a friend tells you about a feeling
column3: listen without laughing and say it makes sense
column4: people feel better when they are understood

column2: getting stuck on hard homework and wanting to give up
column3: take a short break, read the question again, then ask for help
column4: a rested brain sees things it missed before

column2: your Lego model keeps falling apart
column3: check the instructions, try a different way and ask for help if needed
column4: most builders have to try many times

column2: feeling you can't do it
column3: add the word yet: I can't do it yet
column4: abilities grow with practice

column2: feeling lonely at break time
column3: look for someone else alone or join a club or a buddy bench
column4: other children often feel lonely too

column2: feeling lonely in a new town
column3: join a club, team or library group and say hello to neighbours your age
column4: shared activities make new friends

column2: missing a parent who works away or is deployed in the military
column3: write letters, video call, keep a calendar of days and talk about it
column4: keeping in touch makes the distance smaller

column2: feeling bad after you were mean to someone
column3: say sorry and do something kind to make up for it
column4: guilt shows you care, and fixing things lets it go

column2: keeping a secret that you broke something
column3: tell the truth to an adult
column4: lies usually come out later and make it worse

column2: your little brother keeps copying everything you do
column3: be patient; he copies because he admires you
column4: younger siblings learn by watching older ones

column2: arguing with your sister about whose turn it is
column3: use a timer or take turns by agreement, or ask a parent to decide
column4: fair rules stop the same fight happening again

column2: your sibling goes into your room without asking
column3: ask calmly for them to knock and agree house rules with your parents
column4: everyone deserves some private space

column2: your brother or sister gets into trouble and you are tempted to laugh
column3: do not laugh or tease
column4: you would want kindness when it is your turn

column2: telling tales on your sibling for small things
column3: tell an adult only when someone is hurt, in danger or breaking an important rule
column4: telling tales over small things makes others distrust you

column2: a sibling hurts you on purpose
column3: move away and tell a parent
column4: hurting is never okay, even between brothers and sisters

column2: sharing a bedroom with a sibling
column3: agree on quiet times, light-off times and private corners
column4: rules agreed together are easier to keep

column2: feeling that your parents love your sibling more
column3: tell your parents how you feel
column4: parents love each child, and they may not realise how you feel

column2: having a brother or sister with a disability or illness
column3: ask questions, help where you can and tell your parents if you feel left out
column4: families with extra needs work best when everyone shares feelings

column2: your older sibling won't let you join their friends
column3: find your own fun and do something together another time
column4: older siblings need time with friends their age

column2: being left in charge of a younger sibling for a few minutes
column3: keep them in sight and call the adult if anything goes wrong
column4: you are trusted to keep them safe, not to be the parent

column2: a new baby is coming
column3: ask questions about what will change and help prepare
column4: knowing what to expect makes the change easier

column2: the baby cries all the time
column3: be patient; babies cry to tell us they are hungry, tired or uncomfortable
column4: crying is the only way a baby can talk

column2: wanting to hold the new baby
column3: sit down, ask an adult first and support the baby's head
column4: a baby's neck is not strong yet

column2: feeling left out since the baby arrived
column3: ask a parent for one-to-one time and help with the baby if you want
column4: you are still just as important

column2: playing near a sleeping baby
column3: keep quiet and keep small toys away from the baby
column4: babies need lots of sleep and small things can choke them

column2: your parents say no to something you want
column3: ask why and accept the answer, even if you do not like it
column4: parents make rules to keep you safe and healthy

column2: your parents argue loudly
column3: know it is not your fault; go somewhere calm and tell a trusted adult if it frightens you
column4: grown-ups disagree sometimes, and children never cause it

column2: a parent is sad, ill or very tired
column3: be gentle, help a little and tell another trusted adult if you are worried
column4: children can help but should not have to look after a parent alone

column2: a parent works long hours
column3: plan special time together on days off and tell them about your day
column4: sharing your news keeps you close even when time is short

column2: wanting to stay up later than your bedtime
column3: follow the bedtime and ask calmly if it can change as you grow
column4: children your age need about nine to twelve hours of sleep

column2: a parent hurts you or you feel unsafe at home
column3: tell a teacher, school nurse or call a children's helpline
column4: every child has the right to be safe, and adults outside can help

column2: being told to do your homework before play
column3: do the homework first and enjoy play after
column4: finishing jobs first makes free time stress-free

column2: visiting grandparents who live far away
column3: send letters, drawings or video calls between visits
column4: keeping in touch makes them happy and keeps you close

column2: grandparents tell you stories about the old days
column3: listen and ask questions
column4: their stories are family history that only they can tell

column2: a grandparent becomes forgetful
column3: be patient, gentle and remind them kindly
column4: some older people have memory illnesses like dementia; they still love you

column2: grandparents have different rules from your parents
column3: follow the rules of the house you are in, kindly
column4: respecting each home keeps everyone happy

column2: a grandparent can't walk well
column3: offer your arm, walk slowly and help carry things
column4: small help shows care and keeps them from falling

column2: your parents tell you they are getting divorced
column3: know that it is not your fault and that they both still love you
column4: divorce is about the grown-ups' relationship, not about you

column2: living in two homes
column3: keep a calendar and a bag of favourite things for both homes
column4: being organised makes the move between homes easier

column2: one parent says bad things about the other
column3: tell them you love both and do not want to choose
column4: children should not be put in the middle

column2: hoping your parents will get back together
column3: share the feeling but understand it is their decision
column4: most divorces are final, and accepting it helps you heal

column2: being asked to carry messages between parents
column3: politely say they should talk to each other
column4: it is not a child's job to be the messenger

column2: getting a new step-parent
column3: give them time and be polite, even if you are not sure yet
column4: getting close takes time for everyone

column2: having step-brothers or step-sisters
column3: find things you all like doing and give each other space
column4: blended families take time to work out

column2: you are adopted or in foster care and someone asks about it
column3: share only what you want to share
column4: your story is yours to tell or keep

column2: finding out your family is moving
column3: ask questions, look at pictures of the new place and say goodbye properly
column4: knowing what to expect makes it less scary

column2: saying goodbye to friends when you move
column3: swap addresses or contact details through your parents and plan to keep in touch
column4: good friendships can last across distance

column2: your new bedroom feels strange
column3: unpack your favourite things first and arrange the room your way
column4: familiar things help a new place feel like home

column2: learning your new address and phone number
column3: memorise your new address and a parent's number
column4: you may need it if you are ever lost

column2: the first day at a new school
column3: smile, say hello, ask someone's name and ask a teacher if you are lost
column4: everyone feels nervous, and most children are happy to help

column2: you don't know where anything is
column3: ask a teacher or a buddy to show you
column4: schools often have buddies just to help new pupils

column2: a new pupil arrives in your class
column3: say hello, show them around and invite them to play
column4: you would want the same welcome

column2: moving up to a new year group or teacher
column3: visit the classroom if you can and expect the first week to feel strange
column4: change feels strange at first but soon becomes normal

column2: something in your life changes suddenly
column3: talk about it, keep your usual routines and give yourself time
column4: routines help you feel steady

column2: a best friend moves away
column3: keep in touch and stay open to new friendships
column4: you can keep old friends and make new ones

column2: your pet dies
column3: cry if you need, talk about your memories and maybe make a drawing or a little grave
column4: grief is the price of love, and remembering helps

column2: someone says it was only a pet
column3: know that your sadness is real
column4: pets are family members for many people

column2: asking if you can get a new pet straight away
column3: wait a while and talk it through with your family
column4: you need time to grieve, and a new pet does not replace the old one

column2: a grandparent or someone you love dies
column3: ask questions, cry, talk about them and keep a memory box
column4: grief is normal and sharing it helps

column2: wondering if the dead person is just asleep
column3: know that death means the body has stopped working forever and they cannot come back
column4: clear words help children understand, sleeping does not cause death

column2: feeling it was your fault that someone died
column3: know that thoughts and wishes cannot make someone die
column4: young children sometimes believe this, but it is never true

column2: going to a funeral
column3: ask what will happen, sit quietly and it is okay to cry or to be quiet
column4: funerals let people say goodbye together

column2: feeling happy and laughing soon after someone died
column3: know it is fine; grief comes and goes
column4: having fun does not mean you have forgotten them

column2: a friend's family member dies
column3: say I'm sorry and be there for them
column4: simple kindness means more than perfect words

column2: a family member is in hospital
column3: make cards, ask questions and tell an adult your worries
column4: knowing what is happening is less scary than guessing

column2: a parent has a serious illness
column3: keep doing your normal things and talk to a trusted adult
column4: you can still enjoy life and that helps your parent too

column2: making a new friend
column3: smile, ask their name, ask what they like and share something about yourself
column4: friendship starts with interest in each other

column2: a friend tells you a secret
column3: keep it, unless it means someone is in danger or being hurt; then tell a trusted adult
column4: safety is more important than secrets

column2: a friend says something hurtful
column3: tell them calmly how it made you feel
column4: they may not know they hurt you

column2: falling out with your best friend
column3: cool down, then talk and both say sorry if needed
column4: most friendships survive arguments

column2: a friend wants you to break a rule
column3: say no and suggest something else
column4: real friends do not make you do things you know are wrong

column2: a friend keeps being bossy
column3: tell them you want to take turns choosing
column4: good friendships are fair

column2: a friend only plays with you when no one else is around
column3: play with others who treat you well too
column4: real friends are kind all the time

column2: you are not invited to a party
column3: feel disappointed but understand people can't invite everyone
column4: it does not always mean they don't like you

column2: talking about a party in front of people who were not invited
column3: keep party talk quiet
column4: it can make others feel left out

column2: your friend gets a new best friend
column3: stay friendly and spend time with other friends too
column4: friendships change and you can have many friends

column2: you want to stop being friends with someone unkind
column3: be polite but spend less time with them
column4: you don't have to stay close to people who treat you badly

column2: a friend is upset
column3: listen, ask how you can help and keep them company
column4: being there matters more than fixing things

column2: a friend copies your homework
column3: say no kindly and offer to explain it instead
column4: copying does not help them learn

column2: a friend is being bullied
column3: stay with them, tell an adult and do not join in
column4: bullies often stop when others stand up

column2: other children say you can't play
column3: ask an adult on duty or find another group
column4: everyone deserves someone to play with

column2: you notice someone left out of a game
column3: invite them in
column4: including others is kind and makes games more fun

column2: feeling left out of a group chat
column3: tell a parent or teacher; leaving people out online is unkind
column4: exclusion online can hurt as much as in person

column2: being always picked last for teams
column3: tell the teacher how it feels; they can choose teams another way
column4: fair ways to choose stop anyone feeling small

column2: someone keeps calling you names or hitting you
column3: tell a parent and teacher and keep telling until it stops
column4: bullying is never your fault and adults must help

column2: being told not to tell or it will be worse
column3: tell a trusted adult anyway
column4: bullies rely on silence; telling is the way to stop it

column2: seeing someone being bullied
column3: do not laugh or join in; help them away and tell an adult
column4: bystanders who help can stop bullying

column2: someone being mean to you online
column3: do not reply, save the messages and tell an adult
column4: evidence helps adults stop it and replying makes it worse

column2: being tempted to be mean to fit in
column3: do not join in
column4: you can be part of a group without hurting others

column2: being teased about your looks, skin colour, religion or family
column3: tell an adult; this kind of teasing is not allowed
column4: everyone deserves respect for who they are

column2: making a mistake in your work
column3: look at what went wrong and try again
column4: mistakes show you what to learn next

column2: breaking something by accident
column3: tell an adult straight away and say sorry
column4: accidents happen, and honesty is respected

column2: being afraid to try in case you get it wrong
column3: try anyway
column4: you learn far more by trying than by not trying

column2: getting a bad mark on a test
column3: look at what you missed and ask the teacher for help
column4: one bad mark doesn't decide who you are

column2: blaming someone else for your mistake
column3: own up
column4: blaming others is unfair and people stop trusting you

column2: someone else makes a mistake
column3: be kind and don't laugh
column4: you'd want the same kindness

column2: you hurt someone by accident
column3: check they are okay, say sorry and get help if needed
column4: an accident still needs care

column2: saying sorry properly
column3: look at the person, say what you did, say sorry and how you will make it right
column4: a real apology shows you understand

column2: someone says sorry to you
column3: accept it and move on, even if you still feel upset
column4: forgiving helps both of you

column2: you don't understand what the teacher explained
column3: put up your hand and ask, or ask after class
column4: teachers want to help and others probably wonder too

column2: feeling shy about asking for help
column3: remember even adults ask for help all the time
column4: asking for help is smart, not weak

column2: who to ask for help
column3: a parent, teacher, school counsellor, nurse, coach or other trusted adult
column4: having several trusted adults means someone is always there

column2: the first adult you tell does not help
column3: tell another trusted adult
column4: keep telling until someone helps

column2: needing to talk to someone in private
column3: call a children's helpline: Childline 0800 1111 in the UK, Childline 1800 66 66 66 in Ireland, Kids Help Phone 1-800-668-6868 in Canada, Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800 in Australia, Youthline 0800 376 633 in New Zealand, or 988 in the USA
column4: trained people listen for free and in confidence

column2: someone is hurt or in danger right now
column3: call the emergency number: 911 in the USA and Canada, 999 in the UK, 999 or 112 in Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand
column4: emergency services come fast in real danger

column2: a friend asks you to do something dangerous
column3: say no clearly and walk away
column4: your safety matters more than looking brave

column2: someone hugs or touches you and you don't want it
column3: say no or stop and tell an adult
column4: your body belongs to you

column2: a relative wants a kiss and you don't want to
column3: offer a high-five or wave instead
column4: you can choose how you show affection

column2: someone pressures you to share your things
column3: it's okay to say no to some things, but be kind
column4: you choose what is yours to share

column2: someone asks you to keep a secret about touching
column3: tell a trusted adult
column4: no one should ask a child to keep secrets like that

column2: someone online asks for photos or personal information
column3: say no, don't reply and tell a parent
column4: strangers online may not be who they say they are

column2: being asked to try a cigarette, vape or alcohol
column3: say no thanks and walk away
column4: they harm a growing body

column2: someone pushes in front of you in the queue
column3: politely tell them you were there first, or tell an adult
column4: calm words work better than pushing back

column2: someone keeps taking your things
column3: say clearly stop, that's mine, and tell an adult
column4: clear words show you won't be pushed around

column2: a friend is being teased
column3: say that's not kind, stop it and stand with your friend
column4: one voice can change what others do

column2: someone makes an unkind joke about a group of people
column3: say you don't think it's funny
column4: staying silent can seem like agreement

column2: speaking up when you disagree with an adult
column3: be polite and explain your reason calmly
column4: respectful words get adults to listen
